32	def _complex_to_payload(mp: Any, value: Any) -> dict[str, str]:
33	    return {
34	        "real": mp.nstr(mp.re(value), 18),
35	        "imag": mp.nstr(mp.im(value), 18),

40	def _relative_change_payload(mp: Any, low: Any, high: Any) -> dict[str, str | float]:
41	    denom = max(abs(high), mp.mpf("1e-120"))
42	    rel = abs(low - high) / denom
43	    payload: dict[str, str | float] = {"relative_change": mp.nstr(rel, 18)}
44	    if rel > 0:
45	        payload["log10_relative_change"] = float(mp.log10(rel))
46	    else:
47	        payload["log10_relative_change"] = float("-inf")
48	    return payload

51	def observe_cases(mp: Any, cases: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:

1	# Reference Notes: Jacobi Theta Functions
2	
3	These notes summarize the public mathematical conventions used by the task. They are adapted from the mpmath documentation and NIST DLMF Chapter 20.
4	
5	## API convention
6	
7	mpmath exposes the Jacobi theta functions as:
8	
9	```python
10	jtheta(n, z, q, derivative=0)
11	```
12	
13	where `n` is one of `1`, `2`, `3`, or `4`; `z` and `q` may be complex; and a positive `derivative` requests the corresponding derivative with respect to `z`.
14	
15	The nome form assumes `abs(q) < 1`. In that domain the standard theta series are absolutely convergent as mathematical series.
16	
17	## Series definitions
18	
19	For the notation used by this task, the four theta functions may be written as:
20	
21	```text
22	theta_1(z, q) = 2 q^(1/4) sum_{k>=0} (-1)^k q^(k(k+1)) sin((2k+1) z)
23	theta_2(z, q) = 2 q^(1/4) sum_{k>=0}        q^(k(k+1)) cos((2k+1) z)
24	theta_3(z, q) = 1 + 2 sum_{k>=1}        q^(k^2) cos(2 k z)
25	theta_4(z, q) = 1 + 2 sum_{k>=1} (-1)^k q^(k^2) cos(2 k z)
26	```
27	
28	Derivatives with respect to `z` follow by differentiating the sine and cosine factors term by term where the series representation is valid.
29	
30	## Basic checks
31	
32	The functions have parity relations in `z`:
33	
34	```text
35	theta_1(-z, q) = -theta_1(z, q)
36	theta_2(-z, q) =  theta_2(z, q)
37	theta_3(-z, q) =  theta_3(z, q)
38	theta_4(-z, q) =  theta_4(z, q)
39	```
40	
41	Differentiating these identities flips parity according to derivative order.
42	
43	The functions are also periodic or quasi-periodic in the complex argument. These identities are useful scientific checks because two equivalent representations of the same theta-function value should agree within the requested precision.
44	
45	## Relation to the half-period ratio
46	
47	Theta functions are also written with a half-period ratio `tau`, commonly as `theta_n(z | tau)`, with:
48	
49	```text
50	q = exp(pi i tau)
51	```
52	
53	Different references may use different normalizations for the argument and periods. When comparing formulas, keep the `z`, `q`, and `tau` conventions consistent.
54	
55	## Numerical note
56	
57	An absolutely convergent series can still be a poor finite-precision algorithm for some complex inputs. A correct numerical implementation must preserve the value represented by the theta function rather than the accidental behavior of any one intermediate evaluation path.
58	
59	## Public references
60	
61	- mpmath documentation, "Elliptic functions", section `jtheta`.
62	- NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, Chapter 20, "Theta Functions".
63	- NIST DLMF citation guidance lists Release 1.2.7 of 2026-06-15.

and `\vartheta_n = \vartheta_n(0,q)` are also frequently
encountered. Finally, Jacobi theta functions are frequently
considered as functions of the half-period ratio `\tau`
and then usually denoted by `\vartheta_n(z|\tau)`.

def _theta_qseries_all(ctx, n, z, q, nd):

    for j = 0, ..., nd by straightforward floating-point summation of the
    defining q-series, together with per-order norms norms[j] bound to the
    largest magnitude of any summand contributing to values[j].  The norms
    allow callers to measure how many guard bits cancellation may destroy.

    For a fast-converging, well-conditioned call, the summation index is
    started at the center of the fundamental region, i.e. the caller should
    have reduced |Im z| roughly below -log(abs(q))/2, where the successive
    terms shrink monotonically (after a possible single peak for the
    derivative weights (2k+1)**j).
    """
    prec = ctx.prec
    one = ctx.one
    two = ctx.mpf(2)
    iunit = ctx.j
    A = [ctx.zero]*(nd+1)
    T = [ctx.zero]*(nd+1)

    if n in (1, 2):
        zs = z - ctx.pi/2 if n == 1 else z
        q14 = ctx.nthroot(q, 4)
        e1 = ctx.expj(zs)
        e2 = ctx.expj(2*zs)
